title: Caring for Indebted Migrant Workers: Financial Literacy Training, Debt, and Filipino Migrant Workers in Dubai
tldr: Filipino migrant workers in Dubai perform extensive labor to care for their debts, yet financial literacy programs frame indebtedness as individual moral failure rather than addressing structural causes.
problem_and_motivation: Growing levels of debt among Filipino migrant workers in Dubai have prompted civil society organizations to offer financial literacy training as a form of care. These programs assume that debt stems from poor individual financial choices rather than from structural conditions including precarious labor systems and exclusionary banking regulations. There is a gap in understanding how financial literacy education, despite being framed as care, obscures the political economic processes that produce and maintain migrant worker indebtedness.
approach: A multisite ethnographic study was conducted from 2018 onward focusing on IGNITE, a civil society organization providing financial literacy and entrepreneurship training to OFWs in Dubai.
Thirty semi-structured interviews were conducted with current and former IGNITE participants and volunteer mentors based in Dubai and Abu Dhabi.
The analysis follows Raghuram's framework of 'troubling care' to examine how care practices can simultaneously support and constrain migrant workers.
The study situates IGNITE's practices within the broader infrastructure of care for Filipino migrants in the UAE, including Philippine state offices and migrant-led organizations.
The research draws on critical financialization literature to analyze how financial literacy education constructs normative financial subjects.
findings: OFWs perform extensive labors of caring for their debts to survive in Dubai and avoid consequences such as deportation or imprisonment.
IGNITE volunteers acknowledge participants will not master all business know-how in twelve weeks but believe training instills the right 'entrepreneurial mindset.'
Financial literacy training frames OFWs' care expenditures toward family and personal well-being as irresponsible spending that must be curbed.
Personal insolvency settlement procedures exist in the UAE but migrant worker debt remains largely decriminalized, leaving workers vulnerable to passport confiscation, travel bans, and imprisonment.
Some IGNITE participants reported that setting financial goals eased their anxieties and shifted their personal savings priorities.

topic_relevance.contribution_to_field: This paper contributes to migration and financialization scholarship by examining how financial literacy education, despite being framed as care, individualizes migrant indebtedness and obscures structural causes such as precarious labor systems and exclusionary banking regulations. The study reveals the 'hidden geographies' of migrant worker debt by documenting how OFWs in Dubai engage in extensive labors of caring for their debts to survive and avoid legal consequences. The research adds empirical depth to the concept of 'troubled care' by showing how well-intentioned civil society initiatives can reproduce neoliberal financial subjectivities. The paper argues for incorporating migrant debt as an axis of solidarity in efforts to create more just urban spaces for migrants.
directly_justifies: Financial literacy education obscures the political economic conditions that produce and maintain debt among Filipino migrant workers in Dubai.
OFWs engage in labors of caring for their debts not just to survive but to avoid deportation or imprisonment.
IGNITE's training frames OFWs' care expenditures as irresponsible spending that must be curbed.
Personal insolvency legislation in the UAE does not fully decriminalize migrant worker debt.
Debt connects migrant workers and could serve as a basis for future solidarities.
limits: Single case study of one civil society organization limits generalizability to other migrant worker populations or contexts.
Qualitative methodology provides depth but does not measure the scale or prevalence of the phenomena described.
No comparative analysis with similar organizations or programs in other Gulf states or destination countries.
Cross-sectional design does not track changes in participants' financial behaviors or attitudes over time.

limitations: Single case study of one civil society organization limits generalizability to other migrant worker populations or contexts.
Qualitative methodology provides depth but does not measure the scale or prevalence of the phenomena described.
No comparative analysis with similar organizations or programs in other Gulf states or destination countries.
Cross-sectional design does not track changes in participants' financial behaviors or attitudes over time.
remember_this: Filipino migrant workers in Dubai perform extensive labors of caring for their debts to survive and avoid legal consequences.
Financial literacy education, despite being framed as care, individualizes indebtedness and obscures structural causes.
IGNITE's training constrains migrant lives to only hard work and sacrifice by condemning leisure spending as irresponsible.
Personal insolvency laws in the UAE do not fully decriminalize migrant worker debt, leaving workers vulnerable to imprisonment.
Debt could serve as an axis of solidarity among migrant workers if addressed through structural rather than individual interventions.
